newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican opposition parties fail to form alliance.
newsitem.headline: Mexican opposition parties fail to form alliance.

text.p: Mexico's conservative opposition National Action Party (PAN) late on Friday rejected a proposal to join forces with the leftist opposition Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) in July's congressional elections.

Following an 11-hour meeting of top party leaders, PAN President Felipe Calderon announced that his party would reject the PRD's offer to team up against the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

"The PAN will launch its own candidates with our own platform, that is to say not in convergence or in coalition as the law allows," Calderon said in an interview with the television news programme "24 Hours."

The decision was likely to cause relief in the beleaguered ruling party. Its leaders have alternately criticised the proposed alliance as either anti-democratic or a sign that opposition parties lacked confidence to run on their own.
The PRI had no immediate reaction to the decision.
At the same time the PAN's decision came as a disappointment to a growing number of independents and other groups searching for an alternative in Mexican politics.
The Alliance for the Republic, a group of prominent independent political scientists and analysts, said the lack of a PAN-PRD coalition would play right into the PRI's hands.

"The best example of what can happen is found in the experience of the past two years," Alliance leader Santiago Creel told a news conference, ticking off a list of broken promises and political scandals by the ruling party.
"This is what's waiting for us in the three-year period from 1997 to 2000 if the opposition does not gain control of Congress, and it won't without a coalition of parties," he said.

El Barzon, an influential organisation of debtors formed in the wake of Mexico's economic crisis of the past two years, pleaded with the two parties in a statement to join with "progressive and democratic personalities" to defeat the PRI and create "a new course for Mexico."

The PRD, which is not as strong as the PAN, proposed the alliance as a means to achieve their common goal of upsetting the PRI. But the two parties are poles apart ideologically on most issues, with the PAN a fervent backer of free enterprise while the PRD favours government supports and guarantees for the poor.
Pollsters and political analysts have been saying in the run-up to the July elections that the PRI stands to lose its majority in Congress for the first time in 67 years in power.

The PRI, which historically has maintained itself in power through patronage and outright fraud, has seen its popularity plummet because of a severe economic recession and a series of political and corruption scandals in recent years.

Nonetheless, President Ernesto Zedillo has pledged clean elections and made the rule of law a central plank of his administration. When he was easily elected to office in 1994, international observers declared the voting free of fraud.
